title: Coupled universal models for strict constant-coefficient reduction
statement: For a commutative coefficient ring A and an adic coefficient datum d [def-weil-pbc-adic-coefficient-datum], on the original small pro-etale site of any scheme T form the strict inverse sequence M tensor A/I^(n+1), with the quotient transitions and the original constant scalar action [lem-weil-pbc-strict-tower-exchange-mate-normalization]. Package its total left derived functor together with its universal counit and its invertible K-flat computation law as DerivedReductionModelData [def-weil-pbc-derived-reduction-model-data, def-pc-kflat-complex]. Use this coupled model to define reduction, its complex counit, the uniquely normalized augmentation from constant diagrams, and the uniquely normalized exact-pullback comparison. The constructions use the original unequal object and morphism universes.

source.place: Tags 06YY, 0941, 0944 and equation-projection-formula-map (0B56); original-site implementation of fix-lem-exchanges Proof Step 4.

proof.text: The quotient maps and scalar adjunction units define the strict transitions and ordinary augmentation. Tensor-section extensionality and the adjunction Hom equivalence prove uniqueness and transition compatibility.

Apply the existing universal derived-model construction to the strict reduction functor and the independent-coefficient K-flat class. A K-flat resolution resolves every complex. Scalar extension inverts quasi-isomorphisms between K-flat inputs; exact scalar restriction and evaluation do so levelwise. This gives a genuine DerivedReductionModelData value, determined up to its unique counit-compatible isomorphism.

The universal lift of the ordinary augmentation gives the derived augmentation. Its universal factorization gives the complex normalization; cancellation of the K-flat computation counit and a K-flat representative of every derived object prove uniqueness.

Scalar pullback comparisons are mates of the ordinary restriction square. Section formulas prove compatibility with quotient transitions. Descend the resulting strict-tower comparison using the localization of the flat-term K-flat resolving subcategory; cancel its invertible counits there and extend the normalization to every K-flat input by a flat-term refinement.

proof_origin.place: Proof Step 4: original-site constant quotient reduction and its finite perfect projection. The normalization is the counit-tensor mate of Stacks 0B56.

mathlib_searches.query: derived projection formula computed by tensor with a bounded projective complex and a K-injective representative
mathlib_searches.results: Eight results about projective resolutions, K-projectivity and derived objects; no projection-mate normalization or strict-tower theorem.

mathlib_searches.query: The constant sheaf of a perfect coefficient module is represented by a bounded complex of finite free retracts
mathlib_searches.results: Eight results including SheafOfModules.freeFunctor and condensed constant-module functors; no such chain model. Reuse the project finite-projective splitting and constant-exactness APIs.
No hit (project declaration unknown to Mathlib search). The existing project resolving-class theorem and DerivedReductionModelData API were read and reused.

Mathlib has ordinary monoidal adjunction identities and finite-projective splitting. The adopted source has projective lifting and the independent-universe tensorAdjunctionTotal inverse. No matching original-pro-etale reduction-mate computation was found. Whole-DAG search found no existing node for the three new projection specializations.

split_report.summary: Coupled universal models for strict constant-coefficient reduction. The unit route is unchanged; only this original-site implementation is factored.
split_report.duplicate_check: Searched the whole DAG and both Lean roots. The completed-coefficient projection theorem uses a different ring; the generic equal-universe theorem cannot instantiate the original pro-etale site. Reuse their existing abstract tensor and derived-functor ingredients.
